1dw2cwc: Real option, imagined option and advice
smx7fn: To talk about a possible, concrete option, use “si” + present and a consequence in the present or future: “Si nos quedamos en la sala, mantenemos el público fiel”. To imagine an option you haven’t chosen yet and see what would happen, use the conditional: “En una gira llegaríamos a gente que nunca va al teatro”. Never put the conditional after “si”: “si iríamos” is wrong.
chd4lf: To give advice, put yourself in the other person’s place: “Yo que tú, aceptaría”, “En tu lugar, hablaría con el elenco”, “Sería mejor esperar a marzo” (with the infinitive). If you want to name the person, use “es mejor que” + present subjunctive: “Es mejor que lo decidan todos juntos”.

aytgv2: To compare the two options: “Es mejor X que Y”, “Prefiero la gira a la temporada en la sala”, “Por un lado…, por otro…”, “Lo bueno es que…”, “Lo malo es que…”. That way the listener sees the pros and cons before your conclusion.

jkrulv: A good argument has four parts: the thesis (“Creo que debemos salir de gira”), the arguments with connectors (“ya que”, “además”, “incluso”), a counter-argument you acknowledge (“Es verdad que es caro, pero…”, “Aunque perdemos la sala dos meses, …”) and the conclusion (“Así que propongo que…”, “Por eso…”).
k9m2k8: Watch the mood: “creo que”, “me parece que”, “está claro que” and “es verdad que” go with the indicative; “no creo que” and “no me parece que”, with the subjunctive; “es importante que”, “propongo que” and “sugiero que”, also with the subjunctive. To disagree politely: “Entiendo tu idea, pero…”, “No estoy del todo de acuerdo”, “Yo lo veo de otra manera”.
eow6bl: Before you speak, write your thesis in one line and prepare a concession with “es verdad que…, pero…”: people who acknowledge the other side’s argument are more convincing.

mhbxpy: When you argue, your voice marks which word matters. In “No creo que sea CARO, sino que es arriesgado”, the stress falls on the word that contrasts with another. If you put the emphasis somewhere else, the message changes: “No creo que SEA caro” sounds as if you doubt that it is.

1lkwxzt: A week after the meeting, a Montevideo theatre critic publishes this column about La Rambla Teatro’s decision.
dv2jl6: Last week La Rambla Teatro, one of the best-loved independent companies in Ciudad Vieja, put to a vote a question many companies ask themselves: stay in the theatre or go on tour? Most of the cast voted for the tour, and in February they will travel to Salto, Tacuarembó and Rocha. I think it’s a brave decision, and I want to explain why.
tlwb5g: On the one hand, it is clear that independent theatre in Montevideo has a problem: people always perform for the same audience. In an eighty-seat theatre, the people who go are almost always the same, and that, although it is comfortable, doesn’t help anyone grow. On the other hand, in the interior there are magnificent theatres that stand empty for months. The one in Salto, for example, was opened in 1882 and today is perfectly restored, but it receives very few plays a year.
12vvvot: It is true that a tour costs a lot of money and that the Ciudad Vieja theatre will be closed for two months. Some spectators may get annoyed, and the company will most likely earn less than in a normal season. However, I don’t think culture should be measured only in money. If companies don’t leave the capital, the rest of the country will go on seeing theatre only on television.
143t38o: That is why I suggest that the Montevideo council also support these tours, and that other theatres follow the example. If I were them, I would also record the shows in the interior to show them on their return. That way, the regular audience wouldn’t be left without its company, and the new one would have a reason to visit it in the capital.
